identity.title: Midtraining Bridges Pretraining and Posttraining Distributions

problem.claim: Explain what makes midtraining—mixing specialized and general pretraining data in an intermediate phase—effective.

gap.claim: The effectiveness of widespread midtraining practice is poorly understood.

contributions.claim: Proposes viewing midtraining as distributional bridging that improves initialization for posttraining.
Characterizes how domain distance, introduction time, and mixture weight relate to midtraining benefits.
Suggests applying analogous bridging strategies to distributional transitions between other training phases.

stated_novelty.claim: The paper frames midtraining as distributional bridging between pretraining and posttraining distributions.

author_reported_evidence.claim: In controlled pretraining experiments, benefits were largest for domains distant from general pretraining data, including code and math, and increased with the midtraining data’s proximity advantage toward the target distribution.
For code and math-like domains, midtraining consistently outperformed continued pretraining on specialized data alone both in-domain and in mitigating forgetting.
In a code case study, early specialized-data introduction supported higher mixture weights, whereas late introduction required lower weights; introduction time and mixture weight interacted strongly.

narrative_sequence.summary: Midtraining is widespread, but the basis of its effectiveness is not well understood.
The authors propose that midtraining bridges distributions and improves posttraining initialization.
Benefits were strongest for distant domains and exceeded specialized-data-only continued pretraining on in-domain performance and forgetting mitigation.
The code study reports a strong interaction: early introduction permits higher mixture weights, while late introduction requires lower weights.
Late introduction outside a plasticity window may not be recoverable by increasing later data mixtures, motivating bridging across training phases.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links benefit magnitude to domain distance and to a data mixture’s proximity advantage, while separately showing that timing and mixture weight interact.

lessons.interpretation: Training-transition interventions may need to be matched jointly to distributional distance and the model’s stage-dependent plasticity.
lessons.application: When presenting or designing a staged-training method, specify both the transition’s distributional relation and how intervention strength changes with introduction time.
lessons.exception: This framing may be unsuitable when the target transition, plasticity behavior, or distributional proximity cannot be characterized.

unknowns: The abstract gives no quantitative effect sizes, model scales, datasets, or evaluation protocols.
The operational definitions of proximity advantage, forgetting, and the plasticity window are unspecified.
The abstract does not establish whether the proposed bridging view applies beyond the reported domains and settings.
